_note: Content bank for the Logic & Proof Reasons unit inside Geometry Proofs. Truth-table columns use expression trees evaluated by the page code, so answers are computed, not hard-coded. Venn region numbers follow the test paper: 1 = p only, 2 = p and q only, 3 = q only, 4 = p and r only, 5 = all three, 6 = q and r only, 7 = r only, 8 = outside all three. Reason ids refer to data/proofs.json.

drills.statement: If AB + BC = AC and AC = DE + FG, then AB + BC = DE + FG
drills.why: AC is the middle term of a chain: AB+BC equals AC, AC equals DE+FG, so the ends are equal. Segment Addition would need a point between two others giving parts + parts = whole — there is no “between” here, only a chain through AC.
The statement crosses the = / ≅ border. Only the Definition of Congruence is allowed to do that.
Two small adjacent angles add to the big angle. Nobody said BD bisects anything, so the bisector definition does not apply.

drills.statement: Two lines cross, forming vertical angles ∠1 and ∠2. Then ∠1 ≅ ∠2
drills.why: A definition only names the picture. The Vertical Angles Theorem is the if-then that concludes congruence.
This just translates the word “complementary” into “adds to 90°”. The Complement Theorem goes the other way: form a right angle → complementary.

drills.statement: If l ⊥ m, then ∠1 is a right angle
drills.why: ⊥ means perpendicular, not bisector. The Definition of Perpendicular says perpendicular lines form right angles.

drills.statement: If D is the midpoint of CE, then CD = DE
drills.why: Midpoint named → two equal halves. Segment Addition is a different step: CD + DE = CE, which needs a point between two others.

drills.statement: Point D is between C and E, so CD + DE = CE
drills.why: “Between” is the Segment Addition trigger: parts add to the whole. Midpoint would need D to be named as the midpoint and would give CD = DE, not a sum.
A chain of ≅ through a common middle angle. The bisector definition creates one pair of congruent angles; it does not chain two pairs together. Match the symbol: ≅ chain → transitive congruence.
y is REPLACED by x inside an equation. Transitive chains two equalities (A = B, B = C → A = C); substitution swaps a value in.
Flipped — but with ≅, not =. Match the symbol first, then the move.
Both sides were divided by 2. Midpoint is not involved unless a midpoint is named in the step.

lessons.body: “P if and only if Q” (P ↔ Q) means P → Q AND Q → P. One true direction is not enough. Vertical angles are congruent (true), but congruent angles are not always vertical — two 90° angles in different corners are congruent and not vertical. So “congruent iff vertical” is false. “Supplementary iff the sum is 180°” is true both ways, because that is what supplementary means.
lessons.title: Biconditional: both directions must be true
lessons.trap: One direction true ≠ iff true. Always test the reverse.

lessons.body: To disprove “Supplementary angles are never congruent,” one example is enough: 90° + 90° = 180°, and the two 90° angles are congruent. You do not need to check every pair. A conjecture with “never” or “always” only needs a single counterexample to fall.
lessons.title: One counterexample kills a “never” / “always”
lessons.trap: “Never” is a very strong claim. One example breaks it.

lessons.body: p → q is false in exactly one row: p true, q false. Every row with a false antecedent is true — F → F is T, and F → T is T. That is why the third row of p → ~q (p = F, q = T, ~q = F) is T, not F: a false “if” never makes the implication false.
lessons.title: Implication: only T → F is false
lessons.trap: Do not mark F → anything as F. False “if” = true implication.

lessons.body: Read a Venn expression inside out. (~p ∧ r) ∧ q means: inside r, outside p, AND inside q — only region 6 (q and r, not p). “At least 15 credits and NOT a part-time job” means: inside the credits circle, outside the job circle — the left-only crescent, not the overlap.
lessons.title: Venn: ∧ is overlap, ∨ is union, ~ is outside
lessons.trap: ∧ shrinks the region (only the overlap survives). ∨ grows it.

lessons.body: Chain through a middle term (A = B, B = C, so A = C) → Transitive. Swap a value into an equation (RS = WX goes INTO PQ + RS = TV) → Substitution. Flip an equation around → Symmetric. A point between two others giving parts + parts = whole → Segment Addition Postulate. A midpoint named giving two equal halves → Definition of Midpoint. A bisector named giving two congruent angles → Definition of Angle Bisector; chaining two such congruences → Transitive Property of Congruence.
lessons.title: Name the reason: chain, replace, flip, or picture-word?
lessons.trap: Seeing AB + BC = AC does not automatically mean Segment Addition — if the step chains two equalities through AC, it is Transitive.

proofs.given: 2x = y − 2z, x = a − z, y = a + z
proofs.tip: Simplify a + z − 2z to a − z in one clean step before you add anything to both sides. Do not let a half-simplified expression carry into the next line.

proofs.given: Ray PB bisects ∠APC, ray PC bisects ∠BPD (rays in order PA, PB, PC, PD)
proofs.tip: Each bisector definition creates ONE pair of congruent angles. The final step chains them: ∠APB ≅ ∠BPC and ∠BPC ≅ ∠CPD, so ∠APB ≅ ∠CPD. That chain is Transitive Property of Congruence — not another bisector definition.
proofs.title: Angle-bisector proof (new variant — same moves as test Q15)

proofs.given: 2m = n − 2p, m = t − p, n = t + p
proofs.tip: Same moves as test Q13 with new letters. Simplify (t + p) − 2p to t − p on its own line before adding anything to both sides.
proofs.title: Q13-style exercise 1: prove t = p

proofs.given: 3x = y − 2z, x = r − z, y = r + z
proofs.tip: The coefficient 3 means the end needs a division step too: 2r = 2z, so divide both sides by 2.
proofs.title: Q13-style exercise 2: prove r = z

proofs.given: d − 2b = 4c, c = a − b, d = a + b
proofs.tip: This one starts flipped, so the first non-given step is symmetric property: d − 2b = 4c becomes 4c = d − 2b.
proofs.title: Q13-style exercise 3: prove a = b

proofs.given: 5u = v − 2w, u = s − w, v = s + w
proofs.tip: Same pattern, bigger coefficient: finish with 4s = 4w, then divide both sides by 4.

proofs.tip: Here the first given is a sum, not a difference — watch −2b + 2b cancel to 0 in the combine step.

truthTables.label: p → ~q
truthTables.note: The trap row is p = F, q = T: ~q = F, but F → F is T.

truthTables.label: p ∨ (~q ∧ r)
truthTables.note: Work the parentheses first, then the ∨. If p is T, the whole ∨ is T no matter what the second part is.

truthTables.label: (~p ∧ r) ∧ q
truthTables.note: This is the Venn problem in table form: the final column is T only when p = F, q = T, r = T — exactly region 6.

vennProblems.hint: Start with r, throw out everything inside p, then keep only what is also inside q.
vennProblems.label: (~p ∧ r) ∧ q

vennProblems.hint: Inside p, outside q. The overlap with q does not count.
vennProblems.label: p ∧ ~q

vennProblems.hint: Union: everything in q, everything in r, including their overlap.
vennProblems.label: q ∨ r

vennProblems.hint: Outside both p and r. Inside q counts, and so does the outside of all three circles.
vennProblems.label: ~p ∧ ~r

worked.given: 2c = d − 2b, c = a − b, d = a + b
worked.note: The test version went wrong at step 7, turning a + b − 2b into a − b + b. Finish the simplification on its own line, then the last two properties are one move each.
worked.steps: 1. 2c = d − 2b (Given) · 2. c = a − b (Given) · 3. d = a + b (Given) · 4. 2(a − b) = d − 2b (Substitution) · 5. 2a − 2b = d − 2b (Distributive) · 6. 2a − 2b = (a + b) − 2b (Substitution) · 7. 2a − 2b = a − b (Combine like terms: a + b − 2b = a − b) · 8. 2a = a + b (Addition Property: add 2b to both sides) · 9. a = b (Subtraction Property: subtract a from both sides).
worked.title: Test Q13, corrected: prove a = b

worked.given: D is the midpoint of CE
worked.note: The test version wrote CE = CD + DE as step 2 and called it the Definition of Midpoint, then repeated it as step 3. Definition first, addition second — and every substituted value needs its own justified line.
worked.steps: 1. D is the midpoint of CE (Given) · 2. CD = DE (Definition of Midpoint) · 3. CD + DE = CE (Segment Addition Postulate) · 4. DE + DE = CE (Substitution) · 5. 2DE = CE (Combine like terms) · 6. DE = ½CE (Division Property) · 7. ½CE = DE (Symmetric Property).
worked.title: Test Q14, corrected: D is the midpoint of CE, prove ½CE = DE
